paragraphs: An agent’s priorities can change as it consumes or repeatedly encounters something rewarding. This paper studies diminishing marginal utility: receiving more of the same reward can make each additional instance less valuable. That setting differs from a common multitask reinforcement learning setup, where an agent adapts among stationary reward functions drawn from a fixed distribution.

The usual successor representation separates predictions about future state visits from the rewards assigned to those states. This separation supports rapid evaluation of a policy under different reward functions. The authors introduce the λ representation to handle the diminishing-reward setting, and establish that it is required for policy evaluation within that setting. It also generalizes the successor representation and several other existing state representations.

The paper develops the representation’s formal properties and examines its advantages for machine learning and the study of natural behavior. Foraging is a particular focus because the value of continuing to seek a reward can depend on previous consumption. The contribution connects how rewards change with what information a state representation must retain to evaluate behavior.
neurips-2023-a-state-representation-for-.tldr: The λ representation extends successor representations to evaluate policies when repeated rewards have diminishing value.

paragraphs: Combining neural recordings is difficult because different recording sessions capture different neurons, sometimes from different animals. A model cannot simply assume that the same input position refers to the same neuron everywhere. This paper introduces an architecture and training framework for learning shared patterns of neural population activity across these varied recordings.

The method starts by representing individual neural spikes as tokens, preserving fine timing information in an efficient format. Cross-attention and a PerceiverIO backbone then transform these events into latent tokens that represent population activity. This gives the model a way to process diverse recordings through a common internal representation.

The authors train a shared model using recordings from seven nonhuman primates, covering 158 sessions, more than 27,373 neural units, and over 100 hours. Across several tasks, the pretrained model adapts rapidly to unseen sessions with few labels and without specified neuron correspondence. These results support using large collections of recordings to learn reusable neural representations that can reduce the labeled data needed for a new session.
neurips-2023-a-unified-scalable-framewor.tldr: A shared neural decoding model learns across animals and recording sessions, then adapts to new sessions with few labels.

paragraphs: Context can help identify a blurry or partly hidden object, but it can also mislead recognition when an object appears against an unfamiliar background. This paper separates these challenges into Object-Disambiguation, where context is useful, and Background-Invariance, where background information is irrelevant. Models that perform well on one often struggle on the other.

The authors investigate this trade-off through representation geometry and probing methods across a collection of models. They find that better performance on both challenges is associated with more separated object and background representations, together with appropriate weighting of those features. They also manipulate representation factorization and feature weighting, demonstrating causal effects on performance in their tests.

Guided by this analysis, the authors develop augmentation methods that improve both in-distribution and out-of-distribution results over strong baselines. Their findings explain why approaches that improve one kind of contextual robustness can damage another, including some methods for learning causal features. The paper argues for learning distinguishable object and background information and using each appropriately, so context remains available when it helps recognition.
neurips-2023-adaptive-contextual-percept.tldr: Separating object and background representations and weighting them appropriately improves recognition across two competing contextual challenges.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar objects in an image becomes harder when the image’s overall domain also differs from training. These are two distinct changes: a domain shift affects the setting in which familiar content appears, while a semantic shift introduces unfamiliar classes. The paper addresses their joint effect on pixel-level out-of-distribution detection.

ATTA uses two levels of analysis. Global, low-level image features help determine whether the image exhibits a domain shift. Dense, high-level feature maps then identify pixels associated with semantic novelty. Keeping these decisions distinct allows the framework to selectively adapt to unseen domains while strengthening its ability to detect new classes.

The authors evaluate the method on several segmentation benchmarks, including settings with substantial domain changes and settings without them. They report consistent improvements across multiple baseline models. These findings support treating domain adaptation and novel-class detection together: a detector needs to accommodate changes in the image domain while still recognizing that some individual pixels represent content outside its known classes.
neurips-2023-atta-anomaly-aware-test-tim.tldr: ATTA separates image-level domain shifts from pixel-level semantic novelty to improve out-of-distribution segmentation detection.

paragraphs: A generative model can reproduce imbalances in its training data, producing some groups much more frequently than others. This paper targets that imbalance after a generator has already been trained. Its operational goal is semantic uniformity: generating equal numbers of instances from each group defined by the attributes being considered.

The proposed distribution mapping module changes the noise supplied to the generator. It produces samples from a noise distribution designed to make the existing generator’s outputs balanced across those groups. The generator itself does not need retraining, and the procedure does not require access to real training data. This places the intervention at the generator’s input distribution.

Experiments with generators trained on popular real-world datasets show better debiasing performance than existing approaches. The result suggests that altering how a pretrained generator is sampled can address group-frequency imbalances without paying the cost of retraining it. The specific fairness objective here is equal representation among the selected semantic groups, which makes the intended change in generated output explicit.
neurips-2023-debiasing-pretrained-genera.tldr: A learned noise-distribution mapping balances semantic groups in generated outputs without retraining the generator or using real training data.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks use relationships between nodes to make predictions, but those relationships and neighboring attributes can contain sensitive information. Protecting model parameters alone does not resolve every prediction-time privacy concern. Different applications may also require different protections for node attributes and the graph’s connections.

The paper introduces Graph Differential Privacy, a framework that provides guarantees for both model parameters and predictions. A unified definition of neighboring graph datasets supports analysis at different levels of topology protection. The authors show that the graph-convolution-based private models they analyze fail to provide the desired multigranular topology protection and require privacy noise growing at least linearly with maximum node degree.

Their alternative, Differentially Private Decoupled Graph Convolutions, offers more flexible and efficient computation while retaining the framework’s guarantees. Experiments on seven node-classification benchmark datasets and illustrative synthetic data show significantly better privacy–utility trade-offs than existing private GNNs. The contribution links the formal definition of what graph information is protected to an architecture designed to support those distinctions.
neurips-2023-differentially-private-deco.tldr: A graph privacy framework and decoupled convolutions improve control over topology and attribute protection while preserving prediction utility.

paragraphs: Diffusion models are widely designed around static images, whereas forecasting requires representing how a system develops over time. DYffusion connects the steps of a diffusion process directly to temporal dynamics in the data. This gives the forecasting procedure a structure that reflects the kind of change it is trying to predict.

The method trains two components: a stochastic interpolator conditioned on time and a backbone forecasting network. They play roles analogous to the forward and reverse processes in conventional diffusion models. Together, they support predictions across multiple steps and longer time ranges, with flexible sampling trajectories that can move through continuous time.

The design also allows a trade-off between predictive performance and faster sampling during inference. By building temporal dynamics into the process, it introduces a strong inductive bias and improves computational efficiency relative to traditional Gaussian-noise diffusion models. Evaluations on sea surface temperatures, Navier–Stokes flows, and spring mesh systems find competitive probabilistic forecasting scores. These results support using the dynamics themselves to organize diffusion-based forecasting.
neurips-2023-dyffusion-a-dynamics-inform.tldr: DYffusion ties diffusion steps to temporal dynamics to enable flexible, computationally efficient probabilistic forecasting.

paragraphs: Energy-based models offer a flexible way to describe probability distributions, but training them can be computationally demanding. The paper introduces Energy Discrepancy, a loss function that avoids computing scores and avoids expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo. The aim is to make learning these models more practical while preserving a theoretical foundation.

The authors show that Energy Discrepancy approaches explicit score matching and negative log-likelihood in different limits. This connects two established training objectives within one formulation. They further show that minimizing it overcomes the nearsightedness associated with score-based estimation methods and provides theoretical guarantees.

Numerical experiments on low-dimensional distributions find faster and more accurate learning than explicit score matching or contrastive divergence. The paper also addresses a stated obstacle for high-dimensional images: the manifold hypothesis places limitations on this approach. In that setting, the authors demonstrate Energy Discrepancy by training an energy-based prior for a variational decoder model. The evidence therefore includes both direct low-dimensional density learning and a structured use within an image model.
neurips-2023-energy-discrepancies-a-scor.tldr: Energy Discrepancy trains energy-based models without scores or expensive MCMC and connects score matching with likelihood-based learning.

paragraphs: A single observed frame may not contain enough information to predict a physical system’s next state. Unobserved environmental dynamics can make the observed process non-Markovian, meaning its history matters. This paper reframes physical simulation as prediction from a recent trajectory while retaining geometric symmetries such as translations and rotations.

The proposed ESTAG architecture combines spatial and temporal processing in an equivariant graph network. An Equivariant Discrete Fourier Transform extracts periodic patterns from historical frames. A spatial module passes information between graph elements, while a temporal module uses forward attention and equivariant pooling to combine information across time. These components incorporate history while respecting the model’s symmetry structure.

The authors evaluate ESTAG on three real datasets spanning molecular, protein, and macroscopic systems. Results show its effectiveness compared with typical spatiotemporal GNNs and equivariant GNNs. The findings support combining two sources of useful structure: the geometric rules that physical predictions should respect and the past observations needed to recover interactions that a frame-to-frame model can overlook.
neurips-2023-equivariant-spatio-temporal.tldr: ESTAG combines symmetry-preserving graph computation with trajectory history to model physical dynamics affected by unobserved interactions.

paragraphs: In a stochastic linear bandit problem, an algorithm repeatedly chooses actions while learning an unknown reward function. Optimistic algorithms use uncertainty about that function to guide their choices. Their behavior depends on confidence sequences: evolving sets of reward functions that remain plausible as more observations arrive.

This paper constructs tighter confidence sequences using a new tail bound for adaptive martingale mixtures. The statistical result is designed to handle information collected through adaptive decisions. The resulting confidence sets also allow efficient action selection through convex programming, connecting the uncertainty calculation to a tractable decision procedure.

The authors prove that a linear bandit algorithm using these sets achieves competitive worst-case regret guarantees. They show theoretically and empirically that their confidence sequences are tighter than competing ones, and demonstrate improved performance on several hyperparameter-tuning tasks. The contribution is therefore both statistical and algorithmic: more precise uncertainty estimates can improve decisions while retaining a guarantee on accumulated regret in the worst case.
neurips-2023-improved-algorithms-for-sto.tldr: New martingale tail bounds yield tighter confidence sequences and improved linear bandit algorithms with competitive worst-case regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can optimize recommendations for longer-term user rewards, but training and testing directly with users can require substantial resources. KuaiSim provides a simulated user environment for this work. It models multiple kinds of user behavior and responses across sessions, extending the scope beyond a simplified response to one recommendation.

The simulator supports three decision scales. A system can choose a recommendation list for an individual request, optimize a sequence of recommendations throughout a session, or work on retaining users across sessions. Each task comes with evaluation protocols and baseline recommendation algorithms, making the environment a benchmark as well as a place to train models.

The authors rebuild competing simulators on the Kuairand dataset and compare their performance and behavioral differences with KuaiSim. They also deploy KuaiSim on ML-1m to demonstrate flexibility across datasets. These contributions give researchers a common way to examine immediate recommendation behavior and longer-term interaction, with less reliance on online experiments for every stage of development.
neurips-2023-kuaisim-a-comprehensive-sim.tldr: KuaiSim simulates multiple user behaviors across requests and sessions to support training and evaluating long-term recommendation policies.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks underlying causal variables from observations that may combine them in complicated ways. This paper studies a setting with a Gaussian latent distribution and a completely general mixing function. It asks what can be identified when interventions affect hidden variables but the learner does not know their targets.

The authors prove strong identifiability results using unknown single-node interventions. The observations need not be paired counterfactual examples. This extends earlier results restricted to weaker mixing classes or paired data, and establishes identifiability for deep neural network embeddings and general causal structures under the paper’s setting. The Gaussian latent assumption and single-node intervention structure are central parts of that setting.

The proof examines geometric structure that remains in the observed distribution after nonlinear transformation, using quadratic forms of latent precision matrices. The authors also propose a contrastive algorithm for identifying latent variables and evaluate it on several tasks. The contribution combines a theoretical account of recoverability with a practical learning method aimed at recovering the hidden representation.
neurips-2023-learning-linear-causal-repr.tldr: Under Gaussian latent structure, unknown single-node interventions enable causal identifiability despite general nonlinear mixing.

paragraphs: Small molecular datasets often lack enough annotations for effective learning, making additional datasets attractive. However, jointly training on related-looking data can hurt when their tasks differ or conflict. This paper studies how to select auxiliary molecular datasets that are likely to benefit a particular target dataset.

An empirical analysis finds that combining molecular graph similarity with task similarity provides a more reliable indicator of useful auxiliary data. MolGroup builds on that result by representing dataset affinity through separate structural and task components. A routing mechanism assigns gating scores, and bi-level optimization uses meta gradients to adjust that routing toward better target-dataset performance.

The learned affinities guide the choice of a group of datasets for joint training. Across 11 target molecular datasets, the authors report average improvements of 4.41% for GIN and 3.47% for Graphormer when trained with MolGroup-selected data. These findings support making auxiliary-data selection sensitive to both molecular structure and the prediction task, rather than assuming that adding more molecular examples will improve the target model.
neurips-2023-learning-to-group-auxiliary.tldr: MolGroup learns which auxiliary molecular datasets help a target task by combining structural and task affinity.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving random forests need to protect training data while retaining information needed to build useful trees. This paper focuses on Gini impurity, a quantity used during tree construction to assess how mixed the labels are. Its encryption design explicitly preserves the minimum of this learning-relevant quantity.

The scheme modifies a binary search tree so that each node can store several examples. It encrypts data features using both label and ordering information. The authors prove that the minimum Gini impurity is preserved in the encrypted representation without decryption, and provide a security guarantee for their encryption scheme.

For the complete random-forest method, feature encryption uses this specialized scheme, while labels are encrypted with the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme. Experiments examine effectiveness, efficiency, and security and support the proposed method on those dimensions. The central contribution is an encryption design tied to the learning algorithm’s own split criterion, allowing an important part of tree construction to remain meaningful when working with encrypted data.
neurips-2023-on-the-gini-impurity-preser.tldr: A specialized encryption scheme preserves minimum Gini impurity so random forests can retain a key training criterion on encrypted data.

paragraphs: OpenShape learns a shared representation for text, images, and 3D point clouds, aiming to recognize shapes across a broad range of categories. It uses contrastive learning to align these modalities. The paper focuses on scaling the 3D side through larger training collections, improved descriptions, and stronger representation networks.

The authors combine multiple 3D datasets, automatically filter and enrich noisy text, compare ways to scale 3D backbones, and introduce hard-negative mining for more efficient training. OpenShape reaches 46.8% zero-shot accuracy on the 1,156-category Objaverse-LVIS benchmark, compared with less than 10% for existing methods. It also reaches 85.3% on ModelNet40, performing comparably to some fully supervised methods.

The learned representations capture concepts including subcategories, color, shape, and style, supporting fine-grained interactions between language, images, and 3D shapes. Their alignment with CLIP representations also enables integration with existing CLIP-based systems, including point-cloud captioning and image generation conditioned on point clouds. The results show how scaling aligned 3D representations can support both broader recognition and richer cross-modal applications.
neurips-2023-openshape-scaling-up-3d-sha.tldr: OpenShape scales aligned text, image, and point-cloud representations to improve zero-shot 3D recognition and cross-modal applications.

paragraphs: A trained graph neural network can serve as a constraint inside a larger optimization problem, including molecular design. When the optimizer chooses the graph itself, different node numberings can describe the same structure. These equivalent representations create symmetry that complicates the optimization process without introducing genuinely different graph solutions.

The paper proposes two kinds of symmetry-breaking constraints. One establishes the indexing of node zero; the other orders the remaining nodes lexicographically by their neighbor sets. The authors construct a graph-indexing algorithm and prove that its output satisfies the constraints. This establishes that imposing the constraints does not eliminate every symmetric representation of a solution.

For the classical GNN architectures considered, a fixed input graph reduces the problem to optimization over a dense neural network. The authors therefore focus on variable graphs, treating each edge as a decision variable and developing two mixed-integer formulations. They test these formulations and symmetry-breaking strategies in molecular design. The work supplies a way to formulate graph search while controlling redundant node labelings.
neurips-2023-optimizing-over-trained-gnn.tldr: Symmetry-breaking constraints reduce redundant graph labelings in mixed-integer optimization constrained by trained GNNs.

paragraphs: Personalized learning systems estimate students’ knowledge from their past responses, but a new course may provide little evidence about a student. PTADisc supports studying whether information from other courses can help. It brings together 74 courses, 1,530,100 students, 4,054 knowledge concepts, 225,615 problems, and more than 680 million response logs.

Alongside the dataset, the authors introduce a model-agnostic Cross-Course Learner Modeling Framework. It uses relationships between proficiency in different courses to ease diagnosis in cold-start settings. A meta network generates personalized mapping functions between courses, allowing the transfer to reflect the individual student rather than relying on one shared course-to-course mapping.

Experiments on PTADisc report an average AUC improvement of 4.2% for the framework. The paper also benchmarks cognitive-diagnosis and knowledge-tracing models, demonstrating the dataset’s use across diagnostic tasks. Programming logs and student-group information provide additional material for future study. Together, the dataset and framework make cross-course knowledge assessment an experimentally accessible approach to dealing with sparse learning histories.
neurips-2023-ptadisc-a-cross-course-data.tldr: PTADisc and a personalized cross-course mapping framework help estimate student knowledge when a course has little response history.

paragraphs: Synthetic images let researchers choose what appears in a scene and precisely control differences between training and testing data. They can also provide detailed labels and captions. However, insufficient realism has limited their use in representation learning. PUG addresses this tension by combining scene control with photorealistic rendering.

The authors build interactive environments and datasets using Unreal Engine. These environments support controlled image generation, giving researchers a way to vary scene content while retaining knowledge of how each image was produced. That control is valuable for isolating a variable of interest in an evaluation, something that collections of existing real images offer much less directly.

The paper uses PUG for both evaluation and model fine-tuning, demonstrating its potential to improve experimental rigor and training. Its contribution includes the environments as a research tool, not just a fixed image collection. By making realistic scenes controllable, PUG supports experiments in which changes in model behavior can be examined alongside deliberately chosen changes in the input data.
neurips-2023-pug-photorealistic-and-sema.tldr: PUG uses Unreal Engine to create realistic, controllable synthetic images for more rigorous evaluation and improved model training.

paragraphs: A prediction system may sometimes benefit from declining to answer, especially when a wrong answer is costly. This paper studies that choice for regression, where the target is continuous. It gives rejection an explicit cost, so the learning objective balances the cost of predicting poorly against the cost of withholding a prediction.

The authors formulate the expected risk and derive its Bayes-optimal solution. With mean squared error as the evaluation metric, the optimal rule rejects examples whose target variance exceeds the rejection cost. This makes the decision depend on uncertainty in the outcome for an example and on how expensive rejection is within the specified objective.

To train a model, the paper proposes a surrogate loss that treats rejection as a binary classification decision. It supplies conditions for consistency, under which optimizing the surrogate can recover the Bayes-optimal solution. Experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a precise decision rule with a training approach, extending cost-based rejection to continuous predictions while making the role of the chosen loss explicit.
neurips-2023-regression-with-cost-based-.tldr: For squared-error regression, the Bayes-optimal rejection rule compares target variance with rejection cost, and a surrogate loss can recover it under consistency conditions.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces neural-network inference cost by replacing floating-point computation with lower-bit formats. Deploying one approach across devices is difficult because hardware supports particular bit widths. REx addresses this flexibility problem in the data-free setting, where quantization does not depend on access to training data.

The method combines residual quantization error expansion with group sparsity. Its goal is to provide useful accuracy–speed trade-offs across target bit widths and devices. It is also independent of the particular quantization operator, allowing it to work alongside earlier quantization techniques rather than requiring a single fixed conversion rule.

Experiments show better accuracy trade-offs at target bit widths for vision convolutional networks, transformers, and natural-language models. For large language models, the authors report resolving the outlier problem that hampers leading quantization approaches. They also provide theoretical guarantees concerning preservation of the original model’s predictive function. These results connect practical compression flexibility with a formal account of how quantization affects predictions, while supporting use across several model families.
neurips-2023-rex-data-free-residual-quan.tldr: REx combines residual error expansion and group sparsity for flexible data-free quantization across bit widths and model families.

paragraphs: Recognizing invasive species requires distinguishing closely related visual categories, a specialized task that general-purpose vision models do not yet handle well. Existing invasive-species datasets are often small and cover few species. Species196 expands the available data to support development and evaluation of models for this fine-grained recognition problem.

The dataset covers 196 invasive-species categories. Its labeled portion, Species196-L, contains more than 19,000 images with expert-level annotations, while Species196-U contains 1.2 million unlabeled images. This combination supports studying how models use a relatively limited set of accurate labels alongside a much larger collection of images without annotations.

The authors benchmark representative methods through experimental settings that include supervised learning, semi-supervised learning, and self-supervised pretraining. The contribution is a domain-focused dataset and empirical study, providing a common basis for comparing learning approaches. Its scale and category coverage address a stated obstacle to developing automated invasive-species recognition, an application relevant to identifying and managing species with ecological and social consequences.
neurips-2023-species196-a-one-million-se.tldr: Species196 provides expert-labeled and large-scale unlabeled imagery for benchmarking recognition across 196 invasive-species categories.

paragraphs: Recovering 3D information from an ordinary image is harder when the camera’s intrinsic parameters are unknown. This paper estimates the complete four-degree-of-freedom intrinsic parameters from a single undistorted image. Its approach uses learned monocular 3D information instead of relying on calibration objects or strong scene-geometry assumptions.

The authors first show that depth and surface-normal maps determine the intrinsics, but this route requires depth estimates with low bias and variance. They introduce an alternative representation called the incidence field, which describes the rays connecting 3D points with image pixels. It provides a pixel-wise parameterization of the intrinsics that is invariant to cropping and resizing and can be learned from monocular 3D cues.

A robust RANSAC procedure recovers camera intrinsics from the estimated incidence field. The authors report superior performance on synthetic and zero-shot test datasets. They also demonstrate applications in detecting and restoring image manipulations, estimating relative pose from uncalibrated image pairs, and 3D sensing. The contribution makes learned ray geometry the intermediate representation linking an image to its camera calibration.
neurips-2023-tame-a-wild-camera-in-the-w.tldr: A learned incidence field enables recovery of four camera intrinsic parameters from one undistorted image.

paragraphs: Two-team zero-sum games are challenging because teammates share rewards but may hold different information. The TMECor solution concept allows teammates to coordinate strategies before play while forbidding communication during play. Players must therefore use their available information and public actions within those coordination constraints.

Team-PSRO extends policy-space response oracles from two-player games to team games. At each iteration, both teams use reinforcement learning to learn a joint best response to the opposing team’s meta-strategy. A second algorithm, Team-PSRO Mix-and-Match, improves how population policies are used. The convergence guarantee is conditional: Team-PSRO converges to TMECor as its learned joint best responses approach optimal best responses.

Experiments show that a tabular version converges to TMECor in Kuhn poker and Liar’s Dice. A version using deep cooperative reinforcement learning outperforms self-play reinforcement learning in Google Research Football. These findings address both small-game equilibrium learning and performance in a larger game, while preserving the distinction between the conditional theoretical guarantee and the demonstrated large-scale empirical result.
neurips-2023-team-psro-for-learning-appr.tldr: Team-PSRO learns coordinated team strategies with conditional equilibrium convergence and demonstrated gains over self-play in Google Research Football.

paragraphs: High-level synthesis lets developers describe FPGA accelerators in C or C++ and use compiler directives to influence the resulting hardware. Choosing those directives creates a large design space, while evaluating one candidate with synthesis tools can take minutes or hours. Machine-learning predictors can estimate design quality much faster, making suitable training data valuable.

HLSyn is a benchmark intended to improve the complexity and optimization coverage of existing open-source datasets. It contains 42 distinct programs or kernels and more than 42,000 labeled designs. A broader range of optimization pragmas creates varied hardware-design choices for models to learn from and for researchers to evaluate.

The authors compare leading baseline methods for design-quality prediction on this collection. The benchmark’s contribution is a more demanding shared basis for studying prediction in synthesis-driven optimization. It connects model evaluation to programs and directive choices that expand beyond earlier dataset coverage. The authors also describe HLSyn as an ongoing project, with plans to increase both the number and variety of programs.
neurips-2023-towards-a-comprehensive-ben.tldr: HLSyn provides over 42,000 labeled hardware designs to benchmark machine-learning predictions for FPGA high-level synthesis.

paragraphs: Streaming recognition and translation must begin producing output before the full input has arrived. A central decision is when enough source information has been received to generate the next output. Existing methods often encode task-specific rules for this timing, making it harder to learn source-to-target mappings consistently across different sequence types.

Seg2Seg organizes the process around segments. The model alternates between waiting for a source segment and generating a target segment, using a latent segment as the link between them. Its expectation-training procedure explores possible source–target mappings so that generation timing can be learned within the framework.

Experiments across multiple simultaneous generation tasks report state-of-the-art performance and better generality across tasks. The approach matters because output timing is part of the learned mapping, directly addressing the balance between generation quality and latency. A shared segment-based formulation also provides a common structure for tasks such as streaming speech recognition, simultaneous machine translation, and simultaneous speech translation, whose inputs and outputs otherwise differ.
neurips-2023-unified-segment-to-segment-.tldr: Seg2Seg learns when to wait and when to generate through a shared segment-based framework for streaming sequence tasks.
